target: The claim that a federal Election Day holiday would remove voting-time scheduling barriers for low-income workers.
objection: A federal Election Day holiday would not reliably remove those barriers because federal holiday status does not require private employers to give paid time off, and many low-income retail and service workers could still have to work or lose wages to vote.

target: The claim that Election Day should be a national holiday because it would increase participation and civic engagement.
objection: Research shows that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to raise turnout compared with other voting-access reforms, so the holiday is not a reliably effective turnout strategy.

target: The objection that a federal holiday would not remove schedule barriers for low-income workers because private employers are not required to grant paid time off.
objection: Even without a legal requirement for paid leave, federal holidays typically cause school closures and holiday-hour scheduling flexibility that reduces work/school time pressure, so a holiday would still remove many scheduling barriers.

target: The argument that employer time-off laws and automatic voter registration are better substitutes because they are more reliable than a holiday.
objection: Those reforms do not fully substitute for a calendar change: employer time-off laws and automatic registration address different constraints, but a national holiday more comprehensively reduces the work/school scheduling conflict that blocks many voters.

target: The claim that there is no evidence state-by-state reforms can eliminate schedule-related voting barriers.
objection: That is not true, because some states already require employer time off to vote, and evaluations of such laws show they reduce work/time obstacles and can increase turnout among affected workers.

target: The claim that state employer-time-off laws and automatic voter registration are enough to replace a holiday.
objection: Employer time-off requirements and automatic voter registration do not themselves remove work/school schedule barriers in the same comprehensive way as changing the calendar to make Election Day a holiday.

target: The claim that employer time-off laws and automatic voter registration are only inferior substitutes because they do not change the calendar.
objection: Employer time-off laws directly give workers protected time to vote, and automatic voter registration removes registration-timing barriers; together they address the main practical barriers more reliably than a holiday that merely changes the calendar.

target: The claim that voting-access reforms should be preferred instead of a national Election Day holiday.
objection: A holiday should not be rejected in favor of other reforms because the holiday addresses a barrier that those reforms do not fully substitute for, so lawmakers can adopt the holiday as well.

target: The claim that a holiday should be rejected because other reforms are more reliable.
objection: The relevant policy question is not only whether one reform is the single most time-saving access fix, but whether the holiday both increases access and elevates civic participation; on that basis, other reforms do not justify rejecting it.

target: The claim that employer time-off requirements and automatic voter registration adequately replace a holiday.
objection: Those measures do not reliably eliminate the work-and-school scheduling conflicts that a national holiday directly addresses, so they are not sufficient substitutes.

target: The claim that a holiday is needed because employer time-off laws only address work-time barriers while a holiday addresses more.
objection: Employer time-off laws directly remove the work-schedule barrier even without closing schools, and automatic voter registration removes registration-timing barriers, so a package of those reforms addresses the practical barriers without needing a holiday.

target: The claim that employer time-off laws plus automatic voter registration can replace a national holiday.
objection: Employer time-off reforms do not remove school-schedule barriers, and automatic voter registration does not affect school schedules either; a national holiday directly addresses both work and school conflicts.

target: The claim that a national Election Day holiday would reduce work-and-school scheduling barriers and therefore raise participation.
objection: A holiday does not reliably remove work-schedule barriers for low-income workers, because many private-sector retail and service employees still may not get paid time off and could still have to work or lose wages.

target: The claim that a holiday would not meaningfully help low-income workers because their schedules remain inflexible.
objection: A federal holiday typically prompts schools and many employers to adjust schedules or close, which increases flexibility and reduces the likelihood that people must be on their usual shifts.

target: The claim that a holiday would not reliably help low-income workers in inflexible retail and service jobs.
objection: Even if paid leave is not mandated, a federal holiday reduces the likelihood of normal work/school shifts and thus removes many scheduling barriers for low-income workers.

target: The suggestion that a holiday should be rejected in favor of other reforms.
objection: Lawmakers can adopt multiple voting-access and participation measures at the same time, so prioritizing other reforms does not require rejecting a national Election Day holiday.
